newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-OPINION-Louthean on Australian Mining: Kimberley Diamond.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-OPINION-Louthean on Australian Mining: Kimberley Diamond.

text.p: By Ross Louthean*

While the Ashton Mining Ltd -administered Merlin project in the Northern Territory's Batten Trough is the obvious candidate as Australia's next major diamond project to support the world class but maturing Argyle mine, there are some interesting contenders back in the pack.
One that has emerged strongly since the diamond conference is Kimberley Diamond Corp NL (KDC) which listed at the beginning of 1994 as one of the new wave diamond explorers.

KDC has stuck religiously to applying new techniques to earlier conceived diamond prospects and for more than two years the prime focus was the Calwynyardah propsect on an abandoned station between Broome and Fitzroy Crossing in the Kimberleys.

The other property, also acquired from prospectors and mining company executives Graeme Hutton and Terry Allen (who collectively retained 20 percent equity in both properties), was Blina, taking in ground around and generally east of the small Blina oilfield.
Calwynyardah had obvious targets -- huge lamproite pipes, old volcanic vents that can house diamonds, thrust to the surface from eruptive events aeons ago.

But drilling, sampling and other work produced only barely visible microdiamonds at Calwynywardah. While the Calwynywaradh mining camp, set up at the abandoned ruins of the Kimberley cattle station, has now been abandoned there is still hope there for something else -- bentonite, a rich industrial clay for which initial test work is being carried out.
That's not the sort of stuff to put KDC in millionaire lane. That will come from a big commercial cache of diamonds.
BLINA PROSPECT LOOKING EXCITING FOR DIAMONDS

Right now, what was seen by the market as the second string prospect is looking very exciting. From early sampling Blina has producing in just the four bigger stones recovered more than double the carats collected from Calwynyardah's huge pipes.

However, while this has awoken an Australian share market turned impervious over the past two years to junior diamond explorers, it is but the bright lamp that KDC's company secretary, Karl Simich, sees as needing to shine brightly for some time.

Such is the high risk, but high reward play of diamond exploration, with many explorers now turning their attention from the scope for kimberlite and lamproite pipes in far northern Australia for the potential but only theoretically perceived diamondiferous volcanic vents in the granite and greenstone belts of WA's Yilgarn Block -- home of the traditional gold mines in the West.

As Joe Joyce, exploration manager of Stockdale Prospecting -- local arm of the De Beers group -- put it, the greenstones are traditional hosts for gold, while the granites have hardly been touched, therefore providing virginal targets for diamonds in cold cratons, unlike the more recent cratons of the Kimberleys where some kimberlite pipes have been found to have eroded, spreading the diamonds thousands of years ago in an uneconomic distribution for recovery.

Progressive sampling from shallow pits dug on the Blina target area has elevated both interest and KDC's share price as stones anywhere near one carat creates interest, more so in comparing gold exploration, than does a nugget of gold.

However, exploration at Blina in Monopoly terms has not gone much past "Go", for exploration could be described as having reached only the second phase, with the litmus test coming later, possibly during next year's field season, with a start to detailed bulk sampling.

First-pass exploration, involving thousands of shallow holes into this soil covered region of undulating grassland and Brahman and hybrid cattle, has shown a massive palaeochannel river bed (ancient river beds) coming in a wide channel from the Ellendale diamond field and spreading down into a large delta-like area that spreads towards an ancient sea line to the west.
BLINA MAY BE DEPOSITORY FOR DIAMONDS ERODED FROM ELLENDALE

This evidence provides some proof that the Blina area may have been the depository for rich diamonds that eroded with the upper volcanic vents of the big Ellendale lamproite field. This is an area which caused the first big modern diamond rush in Australia when it was uncovered in the 1970s by CRA Ltd in what has become the Argyle Diamond Joint Venture (ADJV).

Millions were spend in closeted exploration at Ellendale but it scaled back when Argyle was found, leaving many diamond seekers to contend the field still has potential. Certainly, the ADJV hasn't discounted the area for it still retains the Ellendale Four and Ellendale Nine pipes which the industry has dubbed as "near commercial" for the giant partnership of RTZ/CRA and Ashton Mining Ltd, and possibly commercial by others who have lower sights and operating costs.

Ellendale Nine is relatively close to the KDC ground and one of the KDC pits that produced the exciting big stones, including the 3.34 carat diamond announced on October 3. At the time of reporting screening had produced 33 stones that collectively totalled about 11 carats, with the three larger accounting for 7.09 carats. This compares with 127 diamonds from Calwynardah which collectively added up to about one carat.

There were two theories developed when KDC took up Blina from vendors Hutton and Allen after Stockdale Prospecting left the area -- that the high incidence of garnets and chrome diopsites spread over a 60 kilometre fan were prime indicators for diamonds shed from Ellendale and also for more deep-seated lamproite pipes.
